item.title: Plastic Straws
item.description: Stop Worrying About Your Consumption Habits
item.content:encoded:
Many people before me have dunked on the plastic-straw Nazis. From a utilitarian perspective, using a paper straw is close to pointless. [1]

Is it worth my mental energy to think about the externalities of my consumption? In the post-singularity utopia, we will price externalities, and no one besides the externality-pricers will have to think about this. For now, if you’re going to think about anything, just let it be your food and travel.

TLDR: These things might matter:

  • Eating meat
  • Traveling long distances[2]
  • Anything that costs a lot of money

Worth zero mental energy:

  • Creating less trash, recycling, composting, buying fewer things
  • Eating organic, eating local
  • Any label that tries to convince me a product is ethical (aside from possibly ones to do with animal welfare)
  • Carbon footprint, outside of travel

I: Methodology #

Probably Approximately Correct #

Claude found basically all of the numbers for this article, and for 20% of numbers it actually told me what I should care about. I strongly believe in the power of working with approximately correct numbers - most of my conclusions don’t change unless Claude was wrong by several OOMs, which doesn’t happen often.

Animal Welfare #

See my thoughts [here](substack todo fix this)

Global Warming #

In my inside view of the world, I care a very small amount about reducing my carbon footprint. I think it’s quite likely we get something singularity-like in the next 20 years. In that time global warming won’t do much harm. But out of epistemic humility, I still try to reduct my carbon footprint.

This post uses GWP20 C02e to model carbon footprint. The gist of it is: how much warming will be caused over the next 20 years by emitting one ton of C02? You can then put other things on the same scale: a ton of methane is ~80 C02e, a flight from SF to NYC is ~2-3 tons C02e (much more than you’d expect from the ~1 ton of pure carbon emissions: physicists think that atmospheric contrails caused by planes have a large warming effect).

It’s convention to use GWP100. I am using GWP20 because I believe that

  1. interest rates are real and your model of the world should account for them. The price of treasuries suggest that $1 today is worth 39c in 2046 and ~.6c in 2126.
  2. the singularity is nigh.

Reader beware: methane (from trash or cows) is ~3x less c02e when using GWP100.

Land Use, Water Use #

I think these things matter, and I tried to quantify how your decisions affect each. But in my heart of hearts, I don’t think you should spend much energy optimizing for either. I think we should just make (a lot more!) national parks and then price and tax land. [3]

II: Things You Shouldn’t Care About #

My main goal in writing this essay was reducing how much I think about my consumption. A list of things you can safely stop worrying about:

Buying Local #

Shipping food in a container on a cargo ship is basically free, economically and from a carbon perspective. In many cases it’s much more environmentally friendly to just ship stuff from where it grows easily.[4]

Wasting Vegan Food #

All of your food carbon footprint is in meat/dairy. Pound for pound, a loaf of bread is ~90× less bad than a steak (~1.4 vs ~120–200 kg CO₂e/kg at GWP20). Buy fresh loaves and toss them when they’re stale.

Reducing, Reusing, Recycling, Composting #

Each year Americans send about 243 million cubic yards of trash to landfill. which means we must create ~1,500 acres of dumps (at 100 ft deep).

After 100 years a landfill gets covered and becomes a park, a golf course, a conservation area, or a solar farm. Assume, conservatively[5], that one acre of new landfill is as bad as 100 acres of farmland.

The average American’s annual landfill use is about 20 cubic feet, or 0.2 ft20.2\ \text{ft}^20.2 ft2 of landfill area. It takes ~1,590 sq ft to create a 1-lb steak, so your year of trash is 0.2/1590×100≈0.0130.2 / 1590 \times 100 \approx 0.0130.2/1590×100≈0.013 steaks: about 1/80th of a steak, even after the 100x penalty.

No one has done a rigorous study showing that microplastics meaningfully impact health. Even if you are worried about them, vanishingly little exposure comes from plastic that properly makes it to landfill.

Warming is also negligible here: The average American’s landfill methane emissions is ~0.53 t CO2e, or about 1/5 of one SF↔NYC round-trip flight or ~10 steaks. And this mostly captured anyway. [6]

Organic foods #

I am not convinced that organic food creates more fewer externalities than normal produce.

Here are Claude’s most important reasons why organic might be worse:

  • It uses a lot more land. Organic yields run ~20-25% lower, so growing the same amount of food takes ~25-33% more farmland.
  • Banning GMOs makes the land problem worse. Organic prohibits GMOs. But GM crops raise yields (killing them drops US corn ~11%, soy ~5%, cotton ~19%).
  • It is not pesticide-free. Organic bans synthetic pesticides but allows a long list of “natural” ones: copper (a heavy metal that never degrades and builds up in soil), sulfur, pyrethrin (toxic to bees and fish), and until ~2007 rotenone (the one they use to give lab rats Parkinson’s).
  • More tillage, more manure. No synthetic herbicides means more plowing for weeds (erosion, diesel), and fertility often comes from manure (a pathogen and runoff vector).

I asked Claude for reasons why Organic farming is better, but it read the above and came up with three bullets that show the opposite. Opus was feeling extra sycophantic today.

  • ~4× fewer synthetic-pesticide residues: (11% of samples vs 46% for conventional). Organic bans synthetic nitrogen fertilizer and cuts cadmium ~in half. Conventonal residues sit well below safety limits, so the personal health case is thin.
  • Farmworker pesticide exposure: Conventional US farms spray ~1 billion lb of synthetic pesticides a year, and globally acute pesticide poisoning hits an estimated hundreds of millions of farmworkers a year (mostly poor-PPE, developing-world farms). But organic farming doesn’t necessarily improve this situation. Sulfur, the primary organic fungicide, is the top reported cause of pesticide illness in California.
  • Biodiversity per acre: Organic fields hold ~30% more species and ~50% more animals. But they need ~30% more land per calorie grown, so you gain ~nothing.

Most Labels On Consumables (eg no bycatch, FSC certified wood) #

Possibly Worthwhile: #

  • Energy Star: Its appliances saved ~520 billion kWh in 2020 (~400 Mt CO₂e, the annual power of ~50M homes), and EPA reckons ~$350 saved per $1 it spent.
  • Certain Animal Welfare Labels: the ones backed by real on-farm audits — Animal Welfare Approved (gold standard: independent auditors visit every farm yearly, the only label Consumer Reports rated “excellent”); Certified Humane (100% pass/fail, on-site audited); Global Animal Partnership (Whole Foods’ 1–5+ steps, higher = better); USDA Organic (real audits, required outdoor access). The tell is a third party auditing the farm: the Animal Welfare Institute found >80% of USDA-approved “animal-raising” claims had no supporting evidence beyond the producer’s own word.

Probably Not Worthwhile: #

  • Dolphin-safe tuna: eastern-Pacific dolphin kills fell ~99% (132,000/yr → ~800). Caveats: that was mostly the 1990 law, and the nets it pushed boats toward kill millions of sharks instead.
  • FSC wood: genuinely mixed — a 2024 Nature study found more wildlife in FSC forests, but Greenpeace quit FSC in 2018, calling it greenwashing.

Definitely Pointless: #

  • Rainforest Alliance: the premium that reaches the farmer is under a penny per chocolate bar (<1% of the cocoa price).
  • Fairtrade: a little more (~1–2¢/bar), but it goes to the co-op, not the farmer.
  • MSC “sustainable” seafood: funded by logo fees on the very products it certifies, and it’s rubber-stamped plenty of contested fisheries.
  • “No bycatch” / “natural” / “eco”: unregulated marketing with no audit behind them.
  • Many Animal Welfare Labels: “Natural” on eggs / meat (meaningless); “No Hormones” on meat (this is banned anyway); “Vegetarian-fed poultry” (chickens are omnivores).

III: An Bucket Of Data, And Things That Might Matter #

Carbon Footprint #

Carbon costs correlate with dollar costs, r = 0.87. If you budget your spending, to some extent you’re already optimizing for reducing externalities.

This is also generally true of land and water use. Graphs for food in particular:

@ Claude we have those three other graphs with just food and cost vs land/water/carbon use Can we plz put just the land and water ones up here please?

Looked at another way: carbon footprint per dollar spent does span two OOMs. This is viewpoint is less comforting.

Quotidian Water Use #

The only thing that matters here is what you eat. Definitely don’t feel guilty about taking a long shower.

Freshwater withdrawals, US, ~2015 (USGS Circular 1441); total ≈ 281 Bgal/day. Biggest omission: thermoelectric power-plant cooling (~130 Bgal/day, ~46%), withdrawn then mostly returned. Landscaping is the outdoor slice of “homes” plus commercial turf; datacenters’ ~0.1 Bgal/day is direct on-site cooling (indirect water via their electricity is several× that — still a rounding error). See below on withdrawals vs. consumption.

US gallons; food/textile figures are total (virtual/lifecycle) water. Steak = 1 lb beef (~1,800 gal), matching the 1-lb steak used elsewhere — a ~½-lb portion is ~900 gal. Almonds: ~1,900 gal/lb is the full LCA footprint (~16,000 L/kg); the viral “~1 gal/almond” (~400 gal/lb) is a narrower blue-water figure. Toilet: ~3.5 gal is an old high-flush unit; modern US toilets are 1.6 gal (WaterSense 1.28). The t-shirt’s ~700 gal is mostly rainfall on cotton, not tap water. Bread ≈ a ~500 g loaf. AI water is operational cooling — ~0.0001 gal/query (Altman’s ~0.32 mL; the viral “~500 mL” figure is per session, not per query), and the $200 plan “used fully” ≈ all-day agentic coding at ~30 kWh/mo.

Agriculture is ~42% of US freshwater withdrawals (nearly all irrigation) and ~80–90% of consumptive use; self-supplied industry is ~5% of withdrawals, and public supply (all homes + businesses) ~12%. Withdrawals vs. consumptive is the key distinction — most home and industrial water is returned to the source, whereas irrigation is mostly consumed.

Charts #

(Need to fix this one)

Appendix #

Recycling #

People will actually pay for recycled cardboard and aluminum, whereas recycled plastic and glass is mostly only used because of mandates or to please consumers.

Here is a table showing how much co2e you can expect so save from recycling various things:

Per ton, by material (US, 2018; “thrown away” = sent to landfill):

material tons landfilled / yr CO2e saved per ton recycled total, if all of it were recycled
aluminum (cans) 1.2M (of 2.7M all aluminum) 9.1 t 11 MMT (24 if all aluminum)
paper & cardboard 17.2M 3.5 t 60 MMT
plastics 27.0M 1.0 t 27 MMT (upper bound)
glass 7.6M 0.3 t 2.3 MMT

Per item:

item CO2e saved by recycling one
1 cubic-foot cardboard box (hollow, single-wall) 0.84 kg (9 Tesla-miles)
1 aluminum can (12 oz) 0.13 kg (1.4 Tesla-miles)
1 glass soda bottle (12 oz) 0.07 kg (0.7 Tesla-miles)
1 PET soda bottle (12 oz) 0.02 kg (0.2 Tesla-miles)

Sources: EPA Facts & Figures 2018 (tonnage), EPA WARM v15 (per-ton CO2e). Per-item weights are assumed — can ≈13 g, box ≈225 g, glass bottle ≈200 g, PET 12 oz ≈15 g — and are the least-certain inputs. These savings are almost all avoided CO2 (smelting/pulping energy), so GWP20 ≈ GWP100 here. “Plastics, if all recycled” is an upper bound: most of those 27M tons have no real recycling path.

Quotidian Power Use #

There were no big surprises for me here. Driving is expensive. AI can use a lot of power, but only if you’re coding with it. Lightbulbs use small but nonzero energy.

(All numbers approximate)

item kWh CO₂e
one ChatGPT/Claude chat query 0.0003 0.1 g
one lightbulb-hour (9W LED) 0.009 3 g
one washer run (cold, machine only) 0.5 0.2 kg
heating the water for a 5-min hot shower 1.1 0.4 kg
one dryer run (electric) 3 1.1 kg
one month of Claude Max ($200) 3 (chat) → tens (all-day agentic coding) 1–11 kg
one Tesla mile 0.25 93 g
one Ford F-150 mile (gas, 20 mpg) 1.7[7] 0.44 kg
average American’s daily lighting (per household) 1.8 0.65 kg
average American’s daily food ill-defined ~10 kg (GWP20; ~6.5 at GWP100)
average American’s daily home use (excl. driving/food, per household) 30 11 kg
average American’s daily driving (per driver, 37 mi) 52[7] 14 kg

  1. My plausible explanations are innumeracy or costly signaling/symbolism (see The Toxoplasma of Rage). ↩︎

  2. Cars and planes use a pretty similar amount of carbon per human mile traveled, but certainly not per human hour spent traveling. ↩︎

  3. Possible using Georgist principles, I’m not sure. ↩︎

  4. Some supermarkets will fly in produce, which seems bad, but I don’t know any heuristics for telling what has been flown (and not trucked or cargo-shipped) besides “avoid sashimi-grade fish from afar and berries with a huge price tag.” ↩︎

  5. It’s actually very generous to the anti-trash side to say that creating an acre of landfill is as bad as creating 100 acres of farmland: discount rates imply that one year of landfill in 2126 is 0.95100=0.6%0.95^{100} = 0.6\%0.95100=0.6% as bad as one year of landfill in 2026. And farmland is fertile land that would counterfactually be biodiverse nature, which is not true of landfill. ↩︎

  6. If you do care, you should put your energy into making sure you recycle your aluminum and cardboard, see appendix. ↩︎

  7. This is fuel energy — the chemical energy in the gasoline — not electricity, so it isn’t apples-to-apples with the EV rows on the kWh column (a gallon of gas holds ~33.7 kWh). The CO₂e column is comparable across every row. ↩︎

item.title: How to Make People Feel Smart
item.description: (And thus ask more questions and learn quickly)
item.content:encoded:
I recently quit my job at a quant trading firm. Early on, we were told explicitly: “the number one mistake new traders make is not asking enough questions.” When I heard this, I thought: “what an easy piece of advice to follow. I’m a curious person, and I’m sociable enough that people won’t mind talking to me, so I bet I’ll ask a ton of thoughtful questions, and learn fast as a result.”

I was wrong. I fell very far behind in learning new things at work because I didn’t ask enough questions. The funny thing was, I knew I was making this mistake. And I couldn’t stop myself. Why is asking questions hard?

One reason you might not ask questions is because you don’t have any. You’re not curious about the thing you’re learning about, your mind is hearing things but not processing, and so you don’t register that there are things you don’t understand fully. This was to some extent true for me at my old job. I find finance more interesting than the average person, but not so interesting that I can spend 55 hours a week thinking about how bond ETFs work and be energized and stimulated the whole time. But this issue was insignificant, in relative terms. I still had tons of unanswered questions I wasn’t asking. Why?

The primary reason I didn’t ask questions at work is because I was embarrassed, ashamed, and self-conscious. For example:

  • Embarrassed when my mentor explained an accounting convention to me and two other new hires, they understood, and I did not.
  • Ashamed when I thought I understood how auctions worked, agreed to be responsible for one, and ended up realizing I didn’t know what was happening and was in the process of making a costly mistake.
  • Self-conscious that I wasn’t performing as well as my peers, and that every time I asked a question other people knew the answer to, I was reminding the room of this fact.

In each of these three scenarios, the correct thing to do next is ask for help:

  • Can you explain that convention one more time?
  • I didn’t realize this was a NASDAQ auction, can someone take over for me?
  • I know we talked about this last week, but can someone remind me what to think about when watching munis?

I knew that I was supposed to ask for help, but my embarrassment, shame, and self-consciousness stopped me dead in my tracks. A piece of advice I thought would be so easy to follow — “ask more questions” — turned out to be tremendously difficult emotionally. I felt like I was a smoker being told to just quit using cigarettes, a chubby kid being told to drop the snickers and have kale for lunch.[1]

Even worse, my employer didn’t do obviously hurtful or aggressive things that made me feel like my fragile emotional state was justified. I was almost never yelled at, never verbally abused or told I was stupid, almost never ranked or explicitly compared to my peers. Still, there are countless subtler signals, verbal and non-verbal, that you express whenever answering a question or explaining a concept. Despite the good intentions of my coworkers, and despite them not doing any of the egregious things listed above, I consistently felt stupid when asking questions and listening to explanations.

Below is the advice I would give to my former coworkers so that future new hires don’t feel the same way. These tips have worked well in my teaching and tutoring experience.[2] Most of the steps below are not actions to take to avoid making someone feel stupid. They are ways you can build people up, actively make them feel smart and valued, and validate that it was good of them to ask a question. Most of my advice is very simple, and yet in my experience ignored more often than not.

You might criticize me by saying that the following this advice will fish out some unnecessary questions. To which I would reply: in your organization, how often do people ask questions that you think are a waste of time? How often do they hold in questions that would have been helpful to ask? In most situations, the latter dwarfs the former, so you should absolutely try to fish out the marginal question that does not get asked.

When someone is asking you questions #

  • Compliment questions, especially good ones, and thank people for asking them.
  • When you don’t know the answer to all or part of a question, draw attention to this fact, so that the person asking thinks the question they’ve asked isn’t a trivial one.
  • Proactively point people to another person who can answer a question in more detail than you, making it easier for them to ask the next person the next question.
  • If someone asks a question that you think other trainees should have asked too, tell them to go share what they learned with the other people you think should hear. This strongly validates the question asked.
  • If you’re busy, don’t just respond to the question in a rushed way. First, communicate that you’re busy, ideally with an apology and some levity. Then respond how you see fit (maybe not at all). That way the person knows that it’s your busy-ness, not the them or their question, that is the issue. When you’re less busy, follow up and make sure that the question got answered; again, you’re demonstrating that the question asked of you was important.
  • If someone asks you a question that you think they could have or should have answered on their own, do not just respond with “I think you can figure that out.” The person asking the question will quickly feel dumb for not figuring out the answer on their own, and embarrassed because they exposed their self-perceived ineptitude by asking the question. If finding the answer really is trivial, you can instead say something like “Have you tried looking at xyz sql table? I think you should be able to get the answer there, let me know if you can’t and I’ll try.” Saying “I’ll try” is usually a lot better than “I’ll show you.” Trying implies that the task is hard and you might fail (even if it isn’t and you won’t), which prevents the asker from feeling like they asked a stupid question.[3]
  • If someone asks you a question that you want them to think about more, don’t just respond with “what do you think?” The person who asked the question could interpret this response as dismissive, thinking you really meant something like “You can answer that on your own, knucklehead. Think before you ask me a question.” Even if you think your tone conveys something else, it’s better to be explicit. Much better responses:
    • I’m not sure about the answer to this question and am curious what thoughts you have.
    • I think this question is an interesting exercise. What have you thought about so far? I think you should consider x. Let me know when you’ve thought more and we can discuss.
  • Show interest in a question and a person by trying to discover where it came from. After thanking or complimenting the question, and maybe also answering it, ask “is this related to xyz project you’re working on?” Or “I’m curious why you’re looking into that.”
  • Once you’ve answered the question, confirm that the person asking understands, patiently. In these final moments, your goal is to make the person you’re talking to you feel like they should have follow up questions (even if you’ve answered this question 100 times before and you think you explained everything perfectly). People always have something they could ask, but they respond to your cues on whether or not they should. Asking “do you have any questions?” is OK, but you can do a lot better. Try:
    • What questions do you have?
    • I glossed over some points there, is there anything I should come back to?
    • This concept is really challenging; I’m sure some of you have questions.

When You Are Giving a Presentation #

  • When people ask questions, thank them, and compliment the question asked.
  • Say at the beginning of the talk that you would like people to ask questions. Tell people that their ideas are welcome and encouraged even if they aren’t fully formed.
  • Be very cautious when describing things as easy, simple, trivial, or straightforward. Often you should just avoid these words entirely. You can call hard things hard without then saying that other things are easy. If you must, referring to a concept as ‘easier’ is better than calling it ‘easy.’ The former leaves room for the interpretation of “all these questions/concepts are hard, I know that, so I’m trying to start with something more manageable.”
  • When you get to a tricky section, acknowledge that the thing you’re about to talk about is complicated/tricky/difficult. Even better, tell the room that you personally struggled with it, or took a long time to figure it out yourself.
  • Stop frequently to ask for questions. After you ask, pause for five seconds and maintain eye contact with the audience. If someone is squirming a little bit like they have a question or are confused, you can say so: “you look like you have a question.” Or “it looks like people are confused.” You can also give people a full minute to digest some counterintuitive point or chunk of math, and then ask for questions. That way students can better formulate questions in their head and feel smarter while asking them.
  • If you suspect people are confused but are too nervous to ask a question or don’t know what to ask, ask the room if they understand. I like to do this by asking people to raise their hand if they feel like they understood.[4]
  • If you feel you’ve botched an explanation, acknowledge that you’ve botched it and try again, more slowly this time.
  • When someone asks a question that might cause you to skip ahead far beyond where most students’ understanding is, or is blatantly designed to make you think they’re clever, or is off topic, make very clear to the class that you do not expect them to have the same depth of understanding that the person who asked the question is displaying. Responding to a challenging, out-of-scope question in the same way that you respond to a normal question makes everyone else in the room think “wow, that other person is way ahead of me. I have a question too, but I don’t want to slow down the class, nor do I want to expose how far behind I am.” You should respond with “that’s an excellent question,” followed by…
    • In short, the answer has to do with x, but the reasoning is quite complicated. I’ll circle back to that if we have time at the end.
    • That’s beyond where I’m hoping to get to today, but come talk to me afterwards and I’m happy to chat more.

In Conclusion #

I think all of the advice I’ve written down is intuitive, maybe even common sense. Nonetheless, it takes practice and effort to do all of these things well. Hopefully reading this reminds you of ways you could be better at building up the self-confidence of those around you, and convinces you to spend a little more of your attention and energy on improving at it.

  1. I feel obligated to mention that me being embarrassed at work is not nearly as difficult a life situation as addiction. I’m not trying to claim that I had it as bad as someone experiencing addiction, just noticing the parallel: in both situations one knows what one should do, and yet cannot bring one’s self to do it. ↩︎

  2. To lend myself some credibility: I was a teaching assistant for five different courses in college and worked part time as a private tutor for five years. ↩︎

  3. If someone is actually asking you questions all the time because they’re too lazy to write a couple lines of code, that’s a separate story. But people normally ask these types of questions by accident and don’t realize how simple the solution is. If you show someone how easy it is to get the answer, they will realize (without you telling them!) and not ask questions like this in the future. Try to be very slow to come to the conclusion that someone is asking you questions because they’re lazy. ↩︎

  4. Raising your hand if you don’t understand is less good, because no one wants to be the first to raise their hand and single themselves out as someone who is lost. Also, people might be sheepish and just keep doing nothing (ie keeping their hands down) as long as everyone else is doing nothing. I would rather falsely believe that people don’t understand than falsely believe that they do. ↩︎
